<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Let $n = 2$ and assume that conditions (1.4) and (1.5) are satisfied. Assume further that $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ is an entire solution of (1.6) together with (1.7). Then, if we require that
\begin{equation}
\mu \ge 3
\end{equation}
holds, $u$ must be an affine function.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
We do not know, if Theorem 1.1 extends to dimensions $n \ge 3$ or if condition (1.8) can be weakened in the sense that the bound $\mu > 1$ is already sufficient for the Calabi-Bernstein property.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Consider functions $a_i : [0, t_i) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, $i = 1,2$, of class $C^2$ on $[0, t_i)$ with numbers $0 < t_i < \infty$ satisfying the conditions (1.4) and (1.5) with $t_0$ replaced by $t_i$ and exponents $\mu_i > 1$ again for $i = 1,2$. Let $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ solve
\begin{equation}
\partial_1 \left( \frac{a_1'(|\partial_1 u|)}{|\partial_1 u|} \partial_1 u \right) + \partial_2 \left( \frac{a_2'(|\partial_2 u|)}{|\partial_2 u|} \partial_2 u \right) = 0 \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R}^2,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
|\partial_i u(x)| < t_i, \quad i = 1,2, \text{ for all } x \in \mathbb{R}^2.
\end{equation}
Then, if for some constant $K > 0$ it holds
\begin{equation}
a_1'(|\partial_1 u|) \le K (a_2'(|\partial_2 u|) + 1) \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R}^2
\end{equation}
or
\begin{equation}
a_2'(|\partial_2 u|) \le K (a_1'(|\partial_1 u|) + 1) \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R}^2,
\end{equation}
$u$ is an affine function.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
According to (1.13), (1.14) some kind of balancing property of the entire solution $u$ implies that $\nabla u = \text{const}$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
With $h$ satisfying (2.1) we let $a$ according to (2.2). Then (1.4) and (1.5) hold with the choice $\mu = 3$, which in particular means that we have the Calabi-Bernstein theorem for problem (1.6) equipped with (1.7).
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Choosing $h(t) = t^2$ in (2.2) we recover problem (1.2), (1.3). The more exotic choice $h(t) := \exp(t) - t - 1$, $t \ge 0$, in formula (2.2) is of course also possible.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
If the function $H : (0, 1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is of class $C^2$ with the properties\begin{equation}\begin{cases}H' > 0, \ H'' < 0 \text{ on } (0, 1], \ \lim_{t \rightarrow 0} H'(t) = \infty, \\lim\inf_{t \rightarrow 0} \frac{-H''(t)}{H'(t)^\mu} > 0 \text{ for some } \mu > 1,\end{cases}\end{equation}then the density $a$ defined in (2.3) satisfies (1.4) and (1.5).
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
If we let $H(t) := t^\alpha$, $0 < t \le 1$, with exponent $\alpha \in (0,1)$, then we obtain (2.4) for $\mu = \frac{2-\alpha}{1-\alpha}$, and if in addition we choose $h(t) = t^2$, then formula (2.3) yields example ii).
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
Consider functions  $a_i : [0, t_i) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ as in Theorem 1.3 and let $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ denote an entire solution of (1.11), (1.12). If $\partial_1 u$ or $\partial_2 u$ does not change sign (i.e. either $\partial_i u \ge 0$ or $\partial_i u \le 0$ for at least one index $i$), then $u$ is an affine function.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We may assume that $\partial_1 u \ge 0$. Recalling $\nabla w = W$ with $W$ defined in (4.2) and remembering that $a_1' \ge 0$ (recall (1.4)) we find that $\partial_2 w \le 0$. Thus the function $w$ is an entire solution of the equation $\text{div}(\nabla f(\nabla w)) = 0$ (notation as in the proof of Theorem 1.3) with $\partial_2 w$ being bounded from one side and the results from [29] imply the constancy of $\nabla w$ and thereby of $\nabla u$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
Let (5.1), (5.2) hold and consider an entire solution $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ of (5.3), (5.4). Assume in addition that $f$ satisfies\begin{equation}\frac{\det D^2 f(q)}{(1 + |\nabla f(q)|)  |D^2 f(q)|} \ge \lambda, \quad q \in \mathcal{O},\end{equation}for some number $\lambda > 0$. Then, if we have\begin{equation}\left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_2}(\nabla u) \right| \le \Lambda \left( \left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_1}(\nabla u) \right|^m + 1 \right) \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R}^2\end{equation}or\begin{equation}\left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_1}(\nabla u) \right| \le \Lambda \left( \left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_2}(\nabla u) \right|^m + 1 \right) \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R}^2\end{equation}with numbers $\Lambda > 0$, $0 < m < 1$, $u$ must be affine.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Recalling definition (5.6) of $\tilde{g}$ and observing that $|D^2 g(p_1, p_2)| = |D^2 \tilde{g}(-p_2, p_1)|$, we get from (5.8) \(|D^{2}g(p)|=\frac{|D^{2}f((\nabla f)^{-1}(-p_{2},p_{1}))|}{\det (D^{2}f((\nabla f)^{-1}(-p_{2},p_{1})))},\quad p\in \mathbb{R}^{2},\) which together with (5.9) ($q = (\nabla f)^{-1}(-p_2, p_1)$) yields \(|D^{2}g(p)|\le \lambda ^{-1}(1+|(-p_{2},p_{1})|)^{-1}=\lambda ^{-1}(1+|p|)^{-1}.\) This shows the validity of (1.5) and (1.6) from [28] for our density $g$. Moreover, (5.10) and (5.11) turn into (1.7) and (1.8) in [28] now for the function $w$, and [28], Theorem 1.1, gives the constancy of $\nabla w$. This implies the constancy of $\nabla f(\nabla u)$ and thereby of $\nabla u$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
